Assigned ScholarRx
Antiviral Drugs: Foundations & Frameworks
Scope note: the official objective says antiviral and antiretroviral mechanisms, but the current Fisher deck is overwhelmingly non-HIV pharmacology. HIV ART remains a separate Week 8 lecture, so this companion does not import the handout's “Beyond the Slides” HIV section into the faculty content.

Slides 2-9: Antiviral Logic Starts With the Viral Life Cycle

Slide 2. Major antiviral targets in the deck: adsorption, uptake/entry/uncoating, and assembly/release/maturation.
Mechanism framework
Block entry • corrupt genome synthesis • prevent protein processing/assembly • prevent release. Antivirals work best when they exploit a viral enzyme or replication step that differs from host-cell biology.
Slide 4. DNA/RNA components. The lecture then walks through nucleic-acid structure before introducing nucleotide analog pharmacology.
Slide 9. Normal DNA formation releases pyrophosphate as DNA polymerase links the next nucleotide. This chemistry becomes the basis for both chain-terminating analogs and foscarnet.
Handout-only clarification: nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate(s). Many antivirals behave as “fake” nucleos(t)ides that are incorporated into viral nucleic acid and terminate elongation.

Slides 10-34: Herpesvirus Antivirals

Acyclovir / Valacyclovir / Famciclovir

Slide 10. HSV uses viral thymidine kinase during DNA replication; this viral kinase becomes the selective activation step for acyclovir.
Slide 11. Acyclovir, ganciclovir, valacyclovir, and penciclovir are shown structurally as guanosine analogs lacking the normal attached ribose sugar.
Slide 14. Acyclovir is first phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase, then by cellular kinases. The slide emphasizes activity in infected cells and therefore lower toxicity.
Slide 15. Once incorporated, acyclovir creates a dead end because the growing DNA chain lacks the OH needed to add the next base.
Acyclovir mechanism
Viral thymidine kinase → acyclovir monophosphate → host kinases → acyclovir triphosphate → viral DNA polymerase incorporates fake guanosine → chain termination.
Slide 16. Valacyclovir is the valine ester of acyclovir. The lecture emphasizes improved intestinal absorption and conversion back to acyclovir in blood.
Slide 17. Famciclovir is converted to penciclovir; the slide emphasizes better absorption/longer half-life and chain termination.
Slide 19. Acyclovir toxicity: crystalluria leading to renal failure, mitigated by hydration/slow infusion, plus neurotoxicity including agitation, delirium, hallucinations, and myoclonus.
DrugCurrent-deck anchorMajor toxicity / pearl
AcyclovirHSV/VZV guanosine analog; viral TK activation; DNA chain terminationCrystalluria / renal failure; neurotoxicity
ValacyclovirValine ester prodrug of acyclovirBetter oral absorption
Famciclovir → penciclovirBetter absorption and long half-life; chain terminationDeck emphasizes structural/pharmacokinetic relationship
Slide 20. Pritelivir appears as an experimental/compassionate-use helicase-primase inhibitor, mechanistically distinct from nucleoside analogs.
Deck-only current emphasis: pritelivir is presented as an experimental compassionate-use helicase-primase inhibitor. Do not flatten it into the acyclovir class.

Ganciclovir / Valganciclovir

Slide 22. Ganciclovir phosphorylation pathway, followed by host-cell kinase activation.
Slide 24. CMV retinitis: ganciclovir is emphasized as much more active than acyclovir; valganciclovir is the better-absorbed valine ester prodrug.
Slide 25. Ganciclovir toxicity: bone-marrow suppression, especially leukopenia; crystalluria is less common than with acyclovir.
CMV drug anchor
Ganciclovir / valganciclovir = CMV • major toxicity = myelosuppression.
Handout-only activation detail: the companion identifies CMV UL97 kinase as the initial activating kinase for ganciclovir and notes UL97 mutation as an important resistance mechanism.

Cidofovir

Slide 26. Cidofovir is shown as an acyclic cytidine monophosphate-like nucleotide analog with a phosphonate group that mimics phosphate.
Slide 28. Broad-spectrum uses shown in the current deck: acyclovir-resistant HSV, adenovirus, HPV, poxvirus, and ganciclovir-resistant CMV.
Slide 29. Cidofovir toxicity is dose-dependent nephrotoxicity with Fanconi syndrome/proximal tubular wasting; the slide lists renal-function contraindication thresholds.
Cidofovir
Nucleotide-like analog → bypasses viral-kinase activation step → resistant herpesvirus option • major problem = proximal-tubule nephrotoxicity / Fanconi syndrome.
Handout-only management pearl: the handout adds coadministration with probenecid + aggressive IV hydration to reduce nephrotoxicity.

Foscarnet

Slide 30. Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog.
Slide 32. Foscarnet blocks normal pyrophosphate-dependent DNA-polymerase chemistry and produces chain termination without needing a nucleoside-activation pathway.
Slide 33. Uses: acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV and CMV when ganciclovir cannot be used.
Slide 34. Current-deck toxicities: crystal deposition, acute tubular necrosis, and nausea with infusion.
Handout-only toxicity enrichment: the handout additionally emphasizes electrolyte disturbances, including hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia, with seizure risk.

Herpes Resistance Logic

ProblemWhy the usual drug failsMechanistic escape
Acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZVLoss/mutation of viral thymidine kinase prevents activationFoscarnet or cidofovir can bypass that kinase requirement
Ganciclovir resistance / intoleranceHandout emphasizes UL97 kinase mutation; myelosuppression may also limit therapyFoscarnet or cidofovir depending context
Ozzy checkpoint - click him once you can answer “which herpes drugs need a viral kinase?” without memorizing isolated lists.
Viral kinase split
Needs viral kinase: acyclovir; ganciclovir.
Does NOT need viral kinase: foscarnet; cidofovir.

Slides 35-42: Ribavirin & Influenza Agents

Ribavirin

Slide 36. Ribavirin is introduced as a purine analog.
Slide 38. The lecture depicts ribavirin as a 'nonsense base' that disrupts nucleic-acid synthesis and chain elongation.
Slide 39. Uses shown: RSV, viral hemorrhagic fevers such as Lassa fever, and 'hepatitis C ???' exactly as written on the current slide.
Do not silently clean up slide 39: the current deck literally places “hepatitis C ???” under ribavirin uses. Treat that as a questioning/historical cue, not as a confident modern HCV recommendation. The HCV section later teaches modern direct-acting antiviral therapy.
Handout-only toxicity enrichment: ribavirin is associated with hemolytic anemia and is a potent teratogen.

Influenza

Slide 40. Current-deck anti-influenza overview: neuraminidase inhibitors and baloxavir, with multiple routes represented.
Slide 41. Neuraminidase-inhibitor toxicity: zanamivir-associated bronchospasm, making it unsuitable for patients with asthma/COPD; confusion is also listed.
Slide 42. Baloxavir toxicities are presented as rare.
Influenza classMechanismHigh-yield use / toxicity
Oseltamivir / zanamivir / peramivirNeuraminidase inhibition → prevents release/emergence of newly formed virionsInfluenza A & B; zanamivir can cause bronchospasm
BaloxavirHandout: cap-dependent endonuclease inhibition / blocks “cap snatching”Deck: toxicities are rare
Handout-only timing pearl: neuraminidase inhibitors are most effective when started early, classically within 48 hours.

Slides 43-53: COVID-19 Pharmacology

Slide 43. The deck re-establishes SARS-CoV-2 as a positive-sense RNA virus before mapping pharmacology onto its life cycle.
Slide 44. Current 2026 risk-based treatment framework: low-risk mild disease gets no antivirals; increasing risk favors nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or remdesivir, with molnupiravir included for high-risk patients.
Slide 45. Remdesivir section begins with the drug's role in SARS-CoV-2 treatment.
Slide 46. Remdesivir is shown as an adenosine monophosphate analog.
Slide 47. Current-deck role: early illness, supplemental oxygen but not critically ill; shortens recovery and lowers progression risk.
Slide 48. Remdesivir toxicities: elevated ALT/AST and infusion reactions such as tachycardia, BP changes, nausea, and rash.
Remdesivir
Adenosine nucleotide analog → inhibits viral RNA polymerase / terminates RNA synthesis • watch liver enzymes + infusion reactions.
Slide 49. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment pair.
Slide 50. Ritonavir inhibits CYP3A, greatly increasing nirmatrelvir concentration; the deck lists dysgeusia, nausea/vomiting, and diarrhea.
Paxlovid interaction logic: ritonavir is there as a pharmacokinetic booster, so CYP3A drug-drug interactions are a central concern.
Slide 51. Molnupiravir is presented as an oral nucleoside-related chain-terminating agent for patients at high risk of serious disease.
Slide 52. Pemivibart: human monoclonal antibody for pre-exposure prophylaxis in moderately to severely immunocompromised patients; binds the spike RBD and blocks ACE2 attachment.
Slide 53. Baricitinib blocks JAK enzymes and reduces inflammatory cytokine signaling; the slide places it in patients requiring supplemental oxygen, mechanical ventilation, or ECMO.
Deck-only distinction: baricitinib is an immunomodulator, not a direct antiviral. It appears in the antiviral lecture because it is part of COVID-19 treatment strategy, but its mechanism is host JAK inhibition rather than direct inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 replication.

Slides 54-58: Hepatitis B

Slide 54. Current deck: entecavir is a guanosine nucleoside analog and tenofovir an adenosine nucleotide analog; both are described as highly effective at suppressing HBV replication.
Slide 55. Entecavir acts as a nonsense-base / chain-terminating analog; listed side effects include headache, fatigue, nausea, and increased liver enzymes.
Slide 56. Tenofovir is shown as an adenosine-monophosphate nucleotide analog.
Slide 57. Tenofovir chain termination; listed adverse effects include GI symptoms, small risk of renal impairment, and decreased bone mineral density.
HBV drugMechanismCurrent-deck adverse effects
EntecavirGuanosine nucleoside analog → chain terminationHeadache, fatigue, nausea, ↑ liver enzymes
TenofovirAdenosine-monophosphate nucleotide analog → chain terminationHeadache, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, small renal risk, ↓ bone mineral density
Slide 58. Bepirovirsen is a current-deck 2026 research update: antisense oligonucleotide targeting all HBV mRNAs, with 24 weeks of subcutaneous injections and modest functional-cure outcomes in the cited studies.
Current-deck update: bepirovirsen is presented as an emerging antisense strategy, not established replacement therapy. Keep the study-result context attached to it.

Slides 59-61: Hepatitis C

Slide 59. HCV disease burden slide sets up why curative direct-acting therapy matters.
Slide 60. Current-deck 8-week combination: glecaprevir (NS3/4A inhibitor) + pibrentasvir (NS5A inhibitor), one pill daily, with >95% cure rate shown.
Slide 61. Current-deck toxicity warning: portal inflammation, especially in HBV co-infection.
HCV suffix anchors
-previr = protease (NS3/4A) • -asvir = NS5A • handout also adds -buvir = NS5B RNA polymerase.
Handout-only safety framing: modern HCV direct-acting antivirals carry an important warning for HBV reactivation; screen for HBV before therapy. The handout also adds NS5B inhibitors such as sofosbuvir, which are not shown in this Fisher slide sequence.

Acyclovir = kidney • Ganciclovir = marrow • Cidofovir = Fanconi kidney • Foscarnet = kidney/electrolytes • Zanamivir = bronchospasm • Remdesivir = liver/infusion • Tenofovir = kidney/bone • HCV DAAs = think HBV reactivation screening.
